strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: extending chain-of-thought reasoning to unified multi-modal (image+text) generation and editing models, where visual state transitions must be modeled alongside textual reasoning.

The macro/micro hierarchical decomposition with dedicated attention masks (hiding intra-subtask reasoning from the macro planner, and restricting micro-level attention to Markovian short-range transitions) is a sensible design for reducing the ~9,000-token-per-step overhead of interleaved visual reasoning, and the reported training efficiency (8 A100 GPUs) is attractive.

Evaluation covers multiple relevant benchmarks (GenEval, WISE, GEdit-Bench, KRIS, RISE), with favorable comparisons against both open-source unified models and commercial systems (e.g., surpassing Gemini 2.0 on KRIS overall).

The 'Nano-Banana like generation' case study (isohypse map -> 3D terrain -> realistic landscape) is an interesting demonstration of decomposed reasoning enabling a capability that direct fine-tuning reportedly fails to achieve.
The supplementary material provides reasonable detail on the data curation pipeline and loss formulations for each auxiliary task.
weaknesses: The submission is explicitly incomplete ('Version 0.2'): the reinforcement learning component is claimed as a core contribution in the abstract and Section 3.3, yet both the main paper and Appendix B.2 state that RL/DPO details 'will be provided in a future version.' Two of the three proposed macro-level planning mechanisms (Parallel Decomposition and Progressive Refinement) are also not implemented or evaluated. A central component of the method is thus unverifiable.

No ablation studies are provided. The contributions of the macro attention mask, micro MDP formulation, the four auxiliary objectives, dataset composition, and the two-stage SFT are not disentangled; 'Uni-CoT Init vs. Uni-CoT' comparisons on GenEval (0.81 vs 0.83) and WISE (0.72 vs 0.75) suggest the reasoning pipeline adds only marginal gains over the base model on some benchmarks, undermining the headline claims.

Potential evaluation contamination/bias: the training data is generated by GPT-4o (prompt enhancement, subtask decomposition, evaluation, and image editing per Figure S2), while several benchmarks are judged by VLM-style evaluators and GPT-4o appears as a comparison system; the paper does not discuss this circularity or benchmark contamination for KRIS/RISE.

Results are mixed and selectively emphasized: on GEdit-Bench the semantic consistency (G SC) score drops substantially relative to BAGEL (6.24 vs 6.83 EN), and on RISE the 'comparable to Gemini-2.0' claim rests on small differences (12.5 vs 13.3) with large gaps to GPT-4o (28.9).

The Nano-Banana case study is purely qualitative on a self-constructed 3K-sample test set with no quantitative protocol, no baseline comparison, and no human evaluation; 'the model converges efficiently and exhibits strong performance on this test set' is unsupported.

Reproducibility is weak: no code or data released at submission time (promised 'shortly'), several key hyperparameters (lambda_CE, number of self-reflection rounds, stopping criteria for the self-reflection loop) are unspecified, and the loop termination condition ('until the model deems the output satisfactory') is undefined.

Presentation quality is below the bar for a top-tier venue: Section 4 contains two 'Experimental Setup' sections (4.2 and 4.3) with duplicated structure, duplicated references ([9]/[10]/[11] Janus-Pro; [38]/[39] Step1X-Edit), typographical errors ('instable training', 'Bagel' vs 'BAGEL', 'Macor attention mask'), and inconsistent benchmark table formatting.

Novelty is moderate: hierarchical task decomposition, self-reflection loops, and MDP-style reasoning are well-established ideas; the main novelty is their combination on top of an existing unified model (BAGEL), and the paper does not clearly delineate its contribution relative to BAGEL-Think beyond benchmark deltas.

strengths: The macro/micro hierarchical decomposition of multi-modal CoT, enforced via explicit macro and micro attention masks, is a sensible and clearly articulated design that directly targets the computational burden of interleaved image-text reasoning (~9K visual tokens per step).

A genuinely useful engineering contribution: the MDP-style formulation of self-reflection with short-range state transitions allows training on modest compute (8 A100 GPUs), which is notable for a unified understanding+generation model.

Broad experimental coverage across both generation (GenEval, WISE) and editing (GEdit-Bench, KRIS, RISE) benchmarks, with reported improvements over the base BAGEL model and strong results on KRIS among open-source models.
The 'Nano-Banana' case study (isohypse map to realistic landscape) is an interesting hypothesis-driven demonstration of decomposition into interpretable visual reasoning steps.
The paper is honest about limitations in Sec. 6, including that parallel decomposition and progressive refinement are unimplemented and that preference learning fails on understanding tasks.
weaknesses: The manuscript is clearly an unfinished draft: the title contains '[Version 0.2: For Nano-Banana Like Generation]', the RL/DPO section states 'Further details on the reinforcement learning setup will be provided in a future version of this work' (and the appendix B.2 is effectively empty), and Secs. 4.2 and 4.3 are both titled 'Experimental Setup'. This level of incompleteness alone is disqualifying for a camera-ready venue.

Limited technical novelty: hierarchical task decomposition, self-reflection loops, attention masking, and DPO fine-tuning are all established techniques. The contribution is largely an application/integration on top of BAGEL rather than a new method, and no component is analyzed in isolation.

No ablation studies. Key design choices (macro attention mask, micro MDP locality, the four auxiliary objectives, data mixture, self-reflection rounds) are never ablated. It is impossible to attribute gains to the proposed components versus simply more GPT-4o-distilled fine-tuning data.

Serious evaluation concerns: (1) the training data is generated by GPT-4o/BAGEL-Think, and several evaluation benchmarks (WISE-style reasoning prompts, KRIS categories) may overlap distributionally with this synthetic data, raising train/test contamination questions that are not discussed; (2) self-reflection quality is judged by the model itself, creating circularity, with no human evaluation anywhere in the paper; (3) results are cherry-presented — on GEdit-Bench, Uni-CoT's SC scores (6.24 EN / 6.30 CN) are substantially worse than BAGEL (6.83/6.85), which is glossed over as 'competitive'; (4) GPT-4o still clearly outperforms Uni-CoT on WISE and RISE, tempering the 'state-of-the-art' claims to 'best open-source'.

No analysis of inference cost/latency. The multi-round generate-then-reflect pipeline multiplies inference compute by many steps, directly contradicting the paper's own motivation about computational burden; the paper only claims cheap training, and never quantifies inference-time overhead versus single-shot generation or Bagel-Think.

Only the sequential decomposition strategy is actually evaluated; the parallel decomposition and progressive refinement strategies promoted in Sec. 3.1 are admitted to be unimplemented, so a third of the proposed method is aspirational.

Qualitative-only evidence for the headline 'Nano-Banana' result (Fig. 6, Sec. 4.5): no quantitative metric, no baseline comparison beyond a screenshot of Google's product, and the claim that direct fine-tuning 'results in unstable training and incoherent generations' is unsupported by any numbers.

Poor presentation quality throughout: duplicated references ([10]/[11], [38]/[39]), typos ('Macor attention mask', 'Bagel', 'preformance', 'are are'), inconsistent claims (abstract says SOTA; tables show otherwise), and missing λ_CE values, hyperparameters for DPO, and evaluation protocols in places.

Only ~11K/20K synthetic trajectories is a small and narrow dataset; generalization claims ('strong generalization') rest on limited out-of-distribution evidence, and the paper itself concedes failure on OOD reasoning trajectories.

strengths: The hierarchical Macro-Level (planning/decomposition) and Micro-Level (MDP-style subtask execution with self-reflection) CoT formulation is a sensible and well-motivated design for reducing the token overhead of multi-modal reasoning, with clear attention-mask mechanics described in the supplementary material.

Evaluation spans several relevant benchmarks (GenEval, WISE, GEdit-Bench, RISE, KRIS), and the method achieves strong results among open-source baselines, including beating the BAGEL base model and competitive performance with Gemini 2.0 on KRIS.
The claim of training on only 8 A100 GPUs via decomposition and short-range attention masks, if verified, would be a practically meaningful efficiency contribution.
The quantitative tables generally include 'Uni-CoT Init' (without reasoning) as an internal control, which is good practice for isolating the effect of multi-modal reasoning.
weaknesses: The paper is explicitly incomplete: key components are deferred to a 'future version' — the entire Reinforcement Learning section says details 'will be provided in a future version of this work' (Sec. 3.3) and Appendix B.2 says the same, and two of the three proposed planning strategies (Parallel Decomposition, Progressive Refinement) are admitted in Sec. 6 to not be implemented. The title even reads '[Version 0.2]', signaling a work-in-progress rather than a finished contribution.

Missing ablations. There is no ablation of the macro/micro attention masks, the MDP formulation, the four auxiliary micro-level objectives, or the dataset composition. The gain of full Uni-CoT over Uni-CoT Init is very small on GenEval (0.81 vs 0.83) and WISE (0.72 vs 0.75), so it is unclear how much of the improvement comes from the proposed reasoning framework versus simply additional fine-tuning data.

The training data is largely distilled from GPT-4o, BAGEL-Think, and similar models (Appendix C), raising concerns that the method is essentially distilling an existing strong model's outputs into a new trajectory format, and creating potential train/test contamination risks on benchmarks like WISE and GEdit-Bench (prompts sourced from similar pools).

Evidence quality is uneven: GEdit-Bench results are mixed (G.SC drops from 6.83 for BAGEL to 6.24), RISE results are described as 'comparable' to Gemini 2.0 despite being lower (12.5 vs 13.3) and far below GPT-4o; the 'Nano-Banana like Generation' section is purely qualitative on a self-constructed 3K test set with no quantitative protocol or baselines.

Reproducibility is currently insufficient: the dataset distribution 'will be detailed in the future', the RL framework details are deferred, and code is only promised 'shortly'. As submitted, key parts of the pipeline cannot be verified or reproduced.

Presentation issues undermine polish: Sections 4.2 and 4.3 are both titled 'Experimental Setup'; Tables S3 appears twice with identical numbering (Macro and Micro tables); the cross-entropy loss is written with a positive sign in Eq. 1 and negative in the appendix; duplicate references ([10]/[11], [38]/[39]); and several results tables have formatting inconsistencies.

Claims sometimes exceed the evidence: 'state-of-the-art performance and strong generalization' is stated in the abstract, but gains over the BAGEL base model are modest on several benchmarks, and OOD generalization is admitted to be problematic in Sec. 6.

strengths: The paper tackles a timely and important problem: extending CoT reasoning to interleaved multimodal settings where visual state transitions must be modeled alongside text, using a unified model (BAGEL) for both understanding and generation rather than loosely coupled pipelines.

The macro–micro hierarchical decomposition with attention masks is a sensible engineering design, and the complexity argument (quadratic to near-linear) is supported by an empirical token-interaction analysis (Figure 4) showing up to 11.26x reduction at 10 reasoning steps.

The evaluation is broad: GenEval, WISE, GEdit-Bench, KRIS, RISE for generation/editing, and MME/MMMU/MMBench/MathVista/Jigsaw-R1 for understanding, plus ablations isolating macro-CoT, micro-CoT, and training strategy contributions.
A base-model generality ablation (replacing BAGEL with BLIP3o) shows the framework transfers across architectures, strengthening the claim that the reasoning paradigm—not the base model—drives gains.

The micro-level self-reflection mechanism with auxiliary objectives (action generation, next-state prediction, reward estimation) is a reasonable recipe for stabilizing interleaved image–text SFT, and training-dynamics comparisons (faster convergence) are provided.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core ingredients (hierarchical task decomposition, self-reflection loops, attention masking to restrict context, SFT on distilled synthetic traces) are all well-established techniques; the MDP formulation is largely notational—rewards are self-generated evaluation scores supervised by cross-entropy, with no actual RL or credit assignment—so the 'MDP-guided' framing overstates the technical contribution.

Headline claims are stronger than the evidence: 'state-of-the-art' is asserted, but on WISE Uni-CoT (0.75) remains below GPT-4o (0.80); on Jigsaw-R1 it is slightly below GPT-4.1-mini (47.60 vs 47.88); and on general understanding benchmarks (MMMU 52.7 vs 52.8, MME essentially unchanged) the improvements over the BAGEL base model are negligible, suggesting the method mainly helps on the specific tasks the training data targets.

Potential benchmark–data alignment concern: the 30K training set is synthesized with GPT-4o/Qwen-plus following exactly the decomposition/self-reflection patterns evaluated on WISE, KRIS, RISE, and jigsaw-style tasks; the paper does not rule out that gains partly reflect distilling GPT-4o onto benchmark-like distributions rather than genuinely better reasoning. No statistical significance or variance reporting is provided.

The complexity analysis, while empirically illustrated, is close to trivial: masking history obviously reduces token interactions, but the paper does not analyze what reasoning capability is lost by restricting attention (e.g., failure cases where long-range coherence across subtasks matters), which is the key trade-off of the hierarchical/Markovian design.

Some results are inconsistent with the narrative: on GEdit-Bench Uni-CoT's G.PQ (6.24) is notably below BAGEL (6.83), and 'improvements largely, mainly relying on our macro decomposition strategy' on GenEval is asserted without a clear causal breakdown; ablations on WISE show only ~0.02-0.04 gains from each component.

Reproducibility is only partially supported: the dataset curation pipeline depends heavily on proprietary models (GPT-4o, Qwen-plus, Gemini comparisons) and the code release is claimed but not verifiable from the manuscript; key details (threshold for self-reflection stopping, λ balancing coefficient, M subtask selection at inference) are underspecified.

strengths: The paper targets a genuine and timely problem: scaling multi-modal chain-of-thought reasoning with interleaved visual and textual states, where token overhead is a real bottleneck.

The hierarchical macro/micro decomposition with attention masking is clearly described, and the empirical token-interaction analysis (Figure 4) reasonably supports the claimed efficiency gains over a naive long-chain baseline.

The training-strategy ablation (Uni-CoT vs. Uni-CoT Raw, Figure 5 / Table S7) and the cross-base-model experiment on BLIP3o (Table S8) show some evidence that the structured trajectory format improves training stability.
Extensive benchmark coverage (GenEval, WISE, GEdit-Bench, RISE, KRIS, Jigsaw-R1, plus general understanding benchmarks) and released code aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: Headline 'state-of-the-art' claims are overstated and inconsistent with the reported numbers: on WISE, Uni-CoT (0.75) is clearly below GPT-4o (0.80), and on Jigsaw-R1 it is below GPT-4.1-mini (47.60 vs 47.88); GenEval gains over the base BAGEL are marginal (0.83 vs 0.79, of which 0.02 already comes without any CoT).

General multimodal understanding results are essentially unchanged relative to the base model (MME identical, MMMU 52.7 vs 52.8, MathVista 73.3 vs 73.1, MMBench 85.6 vs 85.0), which undercuts the claim of broad 'coherent multi-modal reasoning' capability; the large gain is concentrated on Jigsaw-R1, a benchmark whose task style closely matches the training data (jigsaw examples appear prominently in the training trajectories), raising a train-test distribution-overlap concern.

The data pipeline is built almost entirely from GPT-4o/Qwen-augmented and GPT-4o-generated images/annotations over seed prompts sourced from various datasets; no contamination analysis is provided relative to evaluated benchmarks (especially WISE), and the authors themselves concede the data is small-scale, synthetic, and limited in generalization.

Limited conceptual novelty: hierarchical task decomposition, self-refinement, planner/executor splits, and masked/limited-context attention are all well-established; recasting supervised self-reflection as an 'MDP' is mostly notational—no RL or credit assignment is actually involved, and the linear-complexity claim reduces to sliding-window attention, which is a straightforward engineering choice rather than a methodological contribution.

Ablation gains are small and sometimes ambiguous: on GenEval, w/o micro-CoT matches the full model (0.83), and w/o macro-CoT matches w/o CoT (0.81); on WISE the w/o-CoT and w/o-macro rows (0.72/0.73) sit within noise of each other, making component attributions weak.

The complexity analysis counts token interactions but ignores that each visual state still involves ~9-10k tokens and full self-attention within states; no wall-clock latency, memory, or end-to-end inference cost comparison is provided, and the empirical complexity study uses only 100 samples.

Writing and presentation quality issues: typos ('chain-of-though', 'path' vs 'patch' in figures), an incorrectly numbered section structure (Section 8 Reproducibility Statement follows Section 6 with no Section 7), incomplete references (e.g., Pan Lu et al. and Xingchao Liu et al. entries lack years), and the 'Ablation on Training Strategy' paragraph is duplicated verbatim on page 24.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: unified multimodal CoT that interleaves textual reasoning with visual state transitions within a single model (BAGEL), rather than loosely coupling MLLMs with external generators.

The macro-micro hierarchical decomposition with attention masks is a clean, well-motivated design; the complexity analysis (quadratic to near-linear) is clearly formulated and empirically validated (Figure 4 shows token-interaction reductions of 2.24x to 11.26x).

Comprehensive evaluation across both image generation (GenEval, WISE) and understanding (MME, MMMU, MMBench, MathVista, Jigsaw-R1), plus appendix experiments on editing benchmarks (GEdit-Bench, KRIS, RISE); KRIS results notably outperform open-source baselines and Gemini 2.0.

Ablations are reasonably thorough: contributions of macro-CoT vs. micro-CoT are isolated, the training-paradigm ablation (Uni-CoT Raw) shows faster convergence and better final quality, and a second base model (BLIP3o) is used to demonstrate generality of the framework.

Training efficiency is a practical strength: full training in about a week on 8xA100 with a small (30K) dataset, with detailed hyperparameters, data curation pipeline, and a released codebase supporting reproducibility.
Well-written and clearly structured; the MDP framing of micro-level self-reflection and the attention-mask formulation (Figures 2, S1) are easy to follow.
weaknesses: Claims are not always supported by the evidence: on Jigsaw-R1, Uni-CoT (47.60) actually scores below its own base model BAGEL (47.75) and below Qwen3-VL (48.81), contradicting the text's claim that it 'substantially outperforms all compared open-sourced models'. Similarly, gains over BAGEL on GenEval (0.81 to 0.83) and general understanding benchmarks are marginal, with MMMU slightly degrading (34.6 to 32.7).

The complexity reduction is largely an artifact of discarding context via attention masking rather than a genuinely new mechanism; masking history to achieve linear cost trades off information, and the paper does not analyze when this information loss hurts (e.g., tasks requiring cross-subtask visual consistency).

The MDP formulation is superficial: 'reward' is a supervised evaluation score trained with cross-entropy, and there is no RL or closed-loop learning; it is essentially iterative self-refinement with auxiliary supervision, and the framing may overstate the technical novelty.

Training data is heavily synthetic (GPT-4o/Qwen-generated plans, evaluations, and edits), raising concerns about (a) benchmark contamination/shortcut learning on WISE and KRIS, and (b) distillation of GPT-4o behavior rather than emergent reasoning; no decontamination analysis is provided.

Understanding results are mixed and weakly analyzed: the paper attributes WISE vs. GenEval differences in the ablation to prompt 'nature' via hypothesis rather than controlled experiments, and there is no analysis of failure modes or of the self-reflection loop's behavior (e.g., score calibration, stopping criteria, reflection round statistics).

Several important details are deferred to the appendix or under-specified in the main text (threshold for reflection termination, balancing coefficient lambda, how parallel decomposition is actually scheduled at inference).
